# Predicting Weightlifting Exercise Quality Using Random Forest

## 1. Introduction

This project aimed to predict the quality of weightlifting
exercise performance using measurements from wearable
motion sensors. Six participants performed exercises
correctly and incorrectly in five different ways.

The outcome variable, `classe`, identifies five exercise
categories (A, B, C, D, and E).

## 2. Data Preparation

The original dataset contained 19,622 observations
and 160 columns.

I selected 52 motion-sensor measurements from the belt,
arm, forearm, and dumbbell.

I excluded participant identifiers, timestamps,
administrative variables, and measurements with
substantial missing data.

The cleaned dataset contained 52 predictors and
one categorical outcome variable.

## 3. Model Development

I divided the dataset into:

- 75% training data: 14,718 observations.
- 25% validation data: 4,904 observations.

I trained a Random Forest classifier using five-fold
cross-validation.

I compared `mtry` values of 4 and 10 using 150 trees
per forest.

The selected model used `mtry = 10`.

## 4. Model Performance

The model achieved:

- Five-fold cross-validation accuracy: **99.32%**
- Validation accuracy: **99.53%**
- Estimated out-of-sample error: **0.47%**
- Cohen's kappa: **0.9941**

The model correctly classified 4,881 of 4,904
validation observations, making 23 errors.

## 5. Final Predictions

I retrained the final Random Forest model using all
19,622 labelled observations, with 300 trees and
`mtry = 10`.

The model predicted the exercise classes of the
20 unlabelled test observations.

```{r final-predictions}
knitr::kable(
  results,
  caption = "Predicted exercise classes for the 20 test cases"
)
```

## 6. Discussion and Limitations

Random Forest was selected because it can identify
nonlinear relationships and interactions among
motion-sensor measurements.

Five-fold cross-validation was used for model selection,
while the held-out validation set was used to estimate
performance on unseen observations.

One important limitation is that repeated measurements
from the same participants may occur in both training
and validation sets.

Consequently, the estimated error rate may be
optimistic for completely new participants.

A participant-level validation strategy would provide
a stronger assessment of model generalizability.

## 7. Conclusion

The Random Forest classifier achieved 99.53% validation
accuracy and an estimated out-of-sample error of 0.47%.

These results demonstrate that machine learning can
accurately distinguish exercise-performance categories
within this dataset.

Further validation involving previously unseen
participants is necessary before applying the model
to new users.
